open-question.question: In the field measurement that decides whether the completion procedure's read of past work stays discretionary, which outcomes are told apart for each counted run — for instance the named `tasks` command run as shown, a history read the agent composed itself (`git log`, `git blame`, or `git show` on the file), and no history read at all?
open-question.recommendation: It is the one single-outcome classification that shows whether the read is taken as shown, which is what showing the full fixed command is for, so a near-miss form such as `tasks` without `--with-body` gets its own count instead of passing as success; each run still gets one mechanically assigned class, the two failures the draft names stay apart from each other and from every tool read, and the `show` follow-up is kept as a flag.
open-question.alternative: Each counted run gets one outcome from an ordered list, the first matching class winning: the `tasks <path> --with-body` command as shown (the full fixed command, written out literally, on an edited file's path), the milestones tool in another form (`tasks` without `--with-body`, `record` or another query on the file, a relative or variable-held tool path, an alias or function standing for the command), a hand-composed `git log`, `git blame`, `git show`, or `git diff` naming the file (a `git show` of a tool-printed hash being the tool read's follow-up), or no history read. A failed call counts under the form it was written in, and the `show <milestone path>` follow-up is recorded beside the outcome as a yes or no, not as an outcome of its own. It is the only single-outcome classification that measures whether the read is taken as shown, which is what the goal's "full fixed command shown" and the literal-command rule are for, so drift into a near-miss form (the most likely failure for a discretionary step written vaguely) shows as its own count rather than passing as success. The "another form" class needs a hand-maintained list of near-miss spellings that a script has to match, and its value depends on what the procedure demands of the command's spelling, the axis the "Literal-command clause" question owns; the ordering also hides a hand-composed read in any run that called the tool in some form.

Each counted run gets exactly one of two outcomes: the procedure's full fixed `python3 …/tools/milestones.py tasks <path> --with-body` command run on a file the task edits, matched by its command string in the run's tool-call records, or not. Everything else, a milestones-tool call in another form, a history read the agent composed with `git log`, `git blame`, or `git show`, and no history read at all, falls into the one "not run as shown" outcome; the `show` follow-up, a failed call, and a run doing several reads are not told apart. The cheapest and most mechanical classification there is: one string match per run over the tool-call records `host.records` already reads into one shape on all three hosts, with no reader judgment, and it matches the draft's rule exactly where both "never made" and "made by hand" lead to the same result. It cannot tell an agent that hand-rolled a `git log -p` from one that read no history at all, nor a tool call in a slightly wrong form from no read, so the measurement shows that the read failed but not which way, and any result rule that treats the two failures differently has nothing to count; viable only where the rule set under "Result requiring the read" needs no more than made-as-shown against not.

Each counted run gets one of three outcomes: tool read (any milestones-tool `tasks` call on an edited file's path, whatever its spelling, flags, or exit status), hand-composed read (a `git log`, `git blame`, `git show`, or `git diff` the agent wrote naming the edited file's path, a `git show` of a hash the tool's own print supplied counting as the tool read's follow-up and not as hand-composed), or no history read. A run holding both a tool read and a hand-composed read counts as a tool read. It tells apart exactly the three outcomes the draft names ("never made or made by hand"), stays mechanical over the tool-call records, and does not penalize an agent that ran the tool and then followed a printed hash into its diff, the one-`git show` follow-up the `tasks` output is designed to support. A run that took the tool read and also composed its own `git log -p` on the same file reads as a success, so hand-rolling beside the tool, the pattern the tool exists to end, stays invisible, and a `tasks` call without `--with-body` or written through a variable counts the same as the command as shown.

The same three outcomes as above, tool read, hand-composed read, and no history read, with the same rule that a `git show` of a hash the tool printed is the tool read's follow-up, but a run holding any hand-composed read of an edited file's history counts as hand-composed even when it also ran the `tasks` command. It is the strict reading of the draft's failure mode: any composed `git log`, `git blame`, or `git show` on the file is the ad-hoc pattern the tools exist to end, so no run that hand-rolled is counted as a success, while the outcome set stays three classes a script assigns mechanically. An agent that ran the tool and then legitimately widened the read by hand, say `git blame` on a line the task commits did not explain, counts as a failure, which can push the result toward making the read required for behaviour that was the tool read working as intended; the hash-follow-up exemption also needs the script to match hashes against the tool's printed output, which a plain command match does not do.

Each counted run gets one of four outcomes: tool read only, hand-composed read only, both a tool read and a hand-composed read, or no history read, the classes defined as in the three-outcome options (any `tasks` call on an edited file's path is a tool read; a composed `git log`, `git blame`, `git show`, or `git diff` naming the file is hand-composed; a `git show` of a hash the tool printed is the tool read's follow-up), with no precedence rule needed. It keeps the co-occurrence visible instead of resolving it by a precedence the plan has to defend, so the result can tell "agents skip the tool", "agents replace it", and "agents supplement it" apart while each run still gets one mechanically assigned outcome. The "both" class mixes legitimate widening with hand-rolling beside the tool, so a large "both" share still needs a reader to interpret, and like the three-outcome options it counts a `tasks` call in any form, a missing `--with-body` or a call through a variable included, as the tool read.

No single outcome per run: every history read in a counted run is classified and attributed to the edited file it reads, and the run is reported as the set of classes it holds. The classes are the `tasks` command as shown, the milestones tool in another form, the `show <milestone path>` follow-up, a `git show` of a hash the tool printed, a hand-composed `git log`, `git blame`, `git show`, or `git diff` on the file (each git command counted separately), and a failed milestones-tool call; a run holding none of them is the no-history-read run, and any summary outcome is derived from the tallies afterwards. It keeps every distinction a later result rule could need, whatever rule the "Result requiring the read" question settles on, and lets the figures be re-cut later without re-reading the transcripts, the property the earlier measurements lost when their scripts and reports left `temp/`. It is the most work to script and to read: per-file attribution means matching each command to an edited path, the counts no longer answer the question in one line, and a result rule still has to state which tally combination counts as "never made" or "made by hand", so the classification decision is moved onto the result rule rather than settled here.

open-question.question: What measured result makes the completion procedure's read of past work a required step instead of a discretionary one: any counted run in which the read was not taken or was composed by hand, a stated share of the counted runs, or another rule?
open-question.recommendation: Both failures the draft names leave the discretionary mention not producing the tool read and both are cured by a fixed call, so they are pooled; a share tolerates the stray run that makes a one-run threshold a near-certain route to the required form, and setting it under the rates that justified the task-list and fold tools judges this read by the standard the project already acted on, where a majority threshold would leave a 42% failure discretionary.
open-question.alternative: The plan fixes the rule in advance and pools both failure kinds: the read becomes required when the counted runs that took no read or composed their own reach a stated share below half. The share is set low enough to fall under the earlier measured failure rates, for instance one counted run in four. It tolerates an occasional slip but still fires at failure rates like the ones earlier tools were built on: about three in four measured completion agents wrote their own move script, and 42% of measured folds were ad-hoc scripts. A discretionary read failing that often would be judged by the same standard as those earlier hand-rolled steps. The exact share is a judgment fixed before any data exists, and the plan has to defend it. A share only means something over enough runs, which ties it to the minimum run count the measurement-run-set question fixes. It is also open to the same population effect as a zero threshold: if runs where no read was needed are counted, the share rises.

The plan fixes the rule in advance and pools both failure kinds: the read becomes a required step if any single counted run either took no history read or composed its own (a `git log`, `git blame`, or `git show` in place of the named `tasks` command). The threshold is one run. It is the simplest rule to apply, since one run settles it and no share, count, or judgment needs stating. It also matches the draft's sentence "the call never made or made by hand" read run by run, and it treats a hand-rolled read with the same zero tolerance that led to the task-list and fold tools. One outlier run decides the whole question, so the measurement can hardly come out any other way. That makes it a near-certain route to the required form the draft set aside for costing a call on every task. How often it fires depends on the population the sibling question fixes: counted over every completion run, a missed read would be found almost at once even where the trigger never applied.

The plan fixes the rule in advance and pools both failure kinds: the read becomes required only when more than half of the counted runs took no read or composed their own. The read becomes required, and every task pays the call, only once the evidence plainly shows the discretionary form failing in most runs. That is the strongest case for overturning the draft's own reasoning against the required form. A read missed or hand-rolled in as many as 42% of runs (the fold rate that was enough to justify the fold tool) stays discretionary. So the plan accepts a failure rate the project has already treated as reason to act elsewhere. Like any share, it needs the minimum run count the measurement-run-set question fixes.

The plan fixes the rule in advance: the read becomes required only if no counted run took the named `tasks` command as shown, so that the read is never made as written across the whole measurement. This is the draft's "the call never made" read literally, applied to the whole run set rather than run by run. It is the most decisive result possible. If the named command never appears in any counted run, nothing shows that the discretionary mention works, and the case for making the read required is beyond dispute. It almost never fires. One correct run keeps the read discretionary no matter how many other runs skipped it or hand-rolled it, so the measurement would leave in place exactly the silent failure the draft says a discretionary read invites.

The plan fixes the rule in advance and treats the two failure kinds separately. Any counted run that composed its own history read in place of the named command makes the read required by itself. A run that took no read counts toward a stated share below half, and the read becomes required when that share is reached. Each failure kind gets the tolerance it deserves. A hand-composed `git log` is exactly the ad-hoc pattern the full command was shown to prevent, and it is visible in a transcript without any judgment. A run with no read may be a correct skip on a file with nothing behind it, so it is weighed as a rate and not as a single event. Two rules are harder to state and to apply than one, and the zero-tolerance half carries the outlier risk of a one-run threshold. The rule also assumes the measurement tells the two outcomes apart, which the measured-read-outcomes question settles.

The plan fixes the rule in advance and counts only runs that took no history read: the read becomes required when those runs reach a stated share below half of the counted runs. A run that composed its own `git log`, `git blame`, or `git show` counts as having taken the read, so it does not count toward making the step required. The result is matched to the remedy. Making the step required cures a skipped read but not a misspelled one, since a required step can still be written by hand. So only omission is counted against the discretionary form, and a hand-rolled read, which would need a different fix, is not. It departs from the draft's stated rule, which counts a hand-rolled read as a failure. This plan would also give hand-rolled reads no consequence, so the pattern the milestones tool exists to end could persist unmeasured against any threshold. Like any share, it needs the minimum run count the measurement-run-set question fixes.

The plan states what is counted and over which runs but fixes no threshold. The milestone that reads the measurement decides whether the read becomes required, weighing the reported figures as milestones 46 and 48 weighed theirs, against the cost of a call on every task. No number is committed to before the shape of the data is known. That is how the two earlier field measurements were actually used: figures weighed against an estimated saving, not checked against a threshold stated beforehand. It leaves out what the goal says the plan carries, "the result that makes the read required", so it amounts to rejecting part of the goal. It also leaves the outcome open to a reading shaped by whatever the later milestone prefers, the risk a preset rule exists to remove.

open-question.question: Over which runs is the field measurement of the completion procedure's read of past work taken: which projects and hosts, starting from which plugin release, and how many completion runs at the least before its result is read?
open-question.applied-principle: Check tier claims against the live environment
open-question.recommendation: The read is meant for field projects whose files are code, which this repository's prose-heavy, invariant-documented tasks cannot stand in for, and other projects on this machine already hold completion runs in the same transcript store both earlier measurements read; about 200 runs combined matches the 202-transcript completion sample and leaves enough counted runs to read a share, reachable in weeks at this repository's 141 task commits over the last month plus the other projects once a release ships, while a reader per host and a pre-landing baseline add work the result does not use.
open-question.alternative: Projects: this repository plus every other project on this machine running the plugin, as the 88-run answer-sweep measurement of 2026-10-18 spanned seven projects. Hosts: Claude Code only. Start: the landing commit for this repository and, for every other project, the first release that ships this milestone's procedure change (the next after 1.9.0), since those projects install from the distribution repository; no pre-landing baseline. Minimum: on the order of 200 completion runs across the projects combined. Field projects whose files are code rather than plugin prose enter the sample, which is the population the discretionary read is meant to serve, while the sample stays in the one transcript format both earlier field measurements were taken from. The other projects contribute nothing until a release ships and they upgrade, and they hold few or no task commits carrying a bar (a bar stands in the commit body only from milestone 53 on), so many of their runs meet a read that prints little; how many of the combined runs count at all is the run-population question's to decide.

Projects: this repository only. Hosts: Claude Code only, read from its local session transcripts. Start: the commit that lands the rebuilt `hosts/claude/` tree carrying the read, since the maintainer's directory marketplace serves `./hosts/claude` and so runs it before any release; no pre-landing baseline. Minimum: a few tens of completion runs, on the order of 30, before the result is read. The result arrives soonest and from the one project whose task commits carry verified bars and whose files have the deepest task history, so the read has something to surface: this repository landed 141 `Task-completion:` commits over nine active days in the month to 2026-11-10, which puts 30 runs a few working days after the landing. One self-dogfooding project's agents edit mostly plugin prose whose shape `CLAUDE.md`'s invariants already explain, so a few tens of its runs can say little about field projects and leave a low but real rate of skipped or hand-rolled reads unseen; a small sample only settles the question under a sibling rule that a single failing run is enough, which is the result rule's to decide.

Projects: this repository only. Hosts: Claude Code only. Start: the commit that lands the rebuilt `hosts/claude/` tree carrying the read; no pre-landing baseline. Minimum: on the order of 200 completion runs, the size of the 202-transcript completion-agent sample milestone 46 measured on 2026-10-08. A sample the size of the one an earlier completion-procedure decision already rested on, all on the plugin version as built in this tree and in transcripts at hand, so a share-based result rule can be read with the confidence that decision had, with no dependence on other projects upgrading. At this repository's recent pace it takes weeks of milestones to reach, the read staying discretionary all the while, and the sample stays one project's, so it measures how agents behave on this repository's prose-heavy files, not whether field agents on code projects take the read.

Projects: this repository plus every other project on this machine running the plugin. Hosts: all three, Claude Code, Antigravity, and Codex, each read from its own session store and reported per host. Start: the landing commit for this repository and the first release shipping the change (the next after 1.9.0) elsewhere; no pre-landing baseline. Minimum: on the order of 200 completion runs combined, every host's runs counted toward it. The procedure's prose reaches all three hosts but their agents differ (Codex runs its generic subagent told to read the agent file), so this is the only run set that can show a host whose agents never take the read or always hand-roll it, which a Claude-only sample would hide. Each host's transcripts come in their own format, so the measurement needs a reader per host (the host suite's `host.records` shape covers suite runs, not field session stores), and Antigravity and Codex completion runs are likely few, so their per-host figures may stay too small to read.

Projects: this repository plus every other project on this machine running the plugin. Hosts: Claude Code only. Start: the landing commit for this repository and the first release shipping the change elsewhere; no pre-landing baseline. Minimum: no run count; the run set is every completion run made until a fixed number of milestones, on the order of three, have finished in this repository after the landing, and the result is read then. It matches the design draft's own framing, that the read's question is answered by field runs over the milestones that follow, and it ends at a point the plan can name in advance, so the measurement cannot stall waiting on a count. The number of runs it yields is unknown when the plan is written (three milestones may hold a dozen tasks or fifty), so a share-based result may rest on too few runs to read, and the window says nothing about how much the other projects contribute.

Projects: this repository plus every other project on this machine running the plugin. Hosts: Claude Code only. Start: two windows, a baseline of the completion runs already in the transcripts from 2026-10-30, when milestone 53 created the `tasks` query, up to the landing, when agents could have read the record but were not told to; and the measured window from the landing commit here and the first release shipping the change elsewhere. Minimum: on the order of 200 completion runs in the measured window, the baseline taken whole whatever it holds. The baseline is available at once from transcripts already on disk and shows how often agents composed their own `git log`, `git blame`, or `git show` before the procedure named the command, so the measured window's figures read as a change against that rate rather than as a bare number. The baseline spans a different procedure and a mix of plugin versions, so it adds a second set to read and classify for a comparison the result rule may not use, and it inherits the measured window's wait on other projects upgrading; which outcomes are told apart in either window is the read-outcomes question's to decide.
